articles.title: Assam Regiment bags gold at world's toughest patrol exercise
articles.summary: Soldiers of the Indian Army's Assam Regiment have won a gold medal at Exercise Cambrian Patrol 2026, held in Wales in the UK.
articles.body: Soldiers of the Indian Army's Assam Regiment have won a gold medal at Exercise Cambrian Patrol 2026, held in Wales in the UK. The Indian team competed against more than 100 teams from across the world and was among the 10 teams awarded gold medals in one of the most demanding military patrolling exercises anywhere. The Army said the contingent displayed endurance, tactical proficiency, leadership and teamwork and that the result reflects its rigorous training standards and professional competence.Cambrian Patrol is organised by the British Army to assess operational effectiveness, physical endurance and tactical skills under realistic battlefield conditions. Teams spend about 48 hours moving through difficult mountainous terrain while carrying out tasks such as reconnaissance, navigation, casualty evacuation, tactical decision-making and combat drills, all under strict time limits. A typical patrol has eight personnel, who cover around 60 kilometres carrying up to 32 kg each. The tasks can also include crossing obstacles and minefields, gathering intelligence, communications, artillery target procedures and responses to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats.The exercise is not a race with a single winner. Patrols are assessed against military training standards, with gold, silver and bronze medals for different levels of achievement, and a completion award for teams that finish below the medal thresholds. That allows several teams to win gold in the same year. Recent editions have added scenarios involving drones, persistent surveillance and other modern threats, though the emphasis remains on a small team's ability to navigate, gather information and complete its mission under pressure.The Indian Army has taken part for several years, and Gorkha Rifles and Garhwal Rifles units feature prominently in documented results. The 5th Battalion, 1st Gorkha Rifles won Gold in 2007, and the 4/9 Gorkha Rifles won Gold in 2010, followed by another Indian Gold in 2011. The 8th Battalion of the Garhwal Rifles won Gold in 2014, and the Ghatak patrol of the 3rd Battalion, 4th Gorkha Rifles took Silver in 2015. The 2nd Battalion, 8th Gorkha Rifles, won Gold in 2016, and in 2021 the 4th Battalion, 5th Gorkha Rifles (Frontier Force) won Gold after competing against 96 patrols, including 17 international teams. In 2025, the 13th Battalion of the Garhwal Rifles was among the silver medal recipients.Cambrian Patrol began in 1959 as a field-training exercise devised by Welsh Territorial Army soldiers to test basic soldiering skills, including endurance, leadership, navigation, teamwork and marksmanship. Its early format was a long march through Wales followed by a shooting exercise. It grew into an international event, drawing teams from countries including India, Pakistan, the United States, Finland, Estonia and Switzerland among others. It is run by the 160th (Welsh) Brigade in mid-Wales in an area known as the Brecon Beacons.

articles.title: Phase Eight owner hit by cyber-attack as H&M probes separate hack claim
articles.summary: TFG London has apologised to customers for disruption after it identified a "cybersecurity incident" on Sunday.
articles.body:
The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.

According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands".

"We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.

Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.

TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".

The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident.

"As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.

The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly.

"We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.

Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".

Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom.

"No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".

She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".

On Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters.

The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacks including targeting the FBI , Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster.

"We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement.

"At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised."

It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group, via a push notification appearing on their phone screens .

Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note".

It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customers than the retailer initially suggested .

An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

articles.title: Activist Greta Thunberg joins French student protests
articles.summary: Thunberg arrives at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis.
articles.body:
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined the French student protests as more demonstrations calling for better conditions at education facilities are expected nationwide.

Thunberg arrived at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday morning and stood among the students demonstrating.

“Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” Thunberg told the AFP news agency.

Lawyers in robes had also formed a human chain to protect teens following numerous allegations of police brutality at demonstrations.

The protests started late last month as students demanded improvements on a range of issues, including the state of school buildings, a lack of teachers, crowded class schedules and other problems in the education system.

Students have piled up bins and erected security barriers outside hundreds of schools across the country.

Last Thursday, more than 70,000 people took to the streets in the latest major protest event.

Tuesday’s demonstration, backed by unions and a left-wing opposition party, France Unbowed, included a march through Paris and marches in other cities. Pupils clustered outside the doors of several schools in the morning hours, brandishing placards and megaphones and chanting slogans, and marches were planned later in the day.

The university student union, l’Union, said on X: “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them.”

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on France Inter on Tuesday morning that about 200 schools were closed, which was “fewer than last week”, adding that some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage.

The Ministry of National Education also said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, due to the protests.

On Monday, a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, told AFP that “Students aren’t being heard enough … not their proposals to authorities and elected officials.”

He added that the protesters, many being minors, were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”.

Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students are expected to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.

On Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a car show that he urged protesters to exercise restraint.

“These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said.

According to the Ministry of Justice, more than 6,800 people, mainly minors, have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests.

Police have also opened investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.

articles.title: ‘Humans are always fascinated by tragedy:’ How the Titan sub implosion unfolded
articles.summary: When the Titan submersible imploded during its descent to the Titanic wreck in June 2023, Christine Dawood lost her husband and son. Now she’s ready to talk
articles.body: Scrolling through Instagram during the Covid lockdown, Christine Dawood saw something that made her do a double take. “I just thought, ‘That’s fake,’” she remembers. She passed her phone to her husband — not out of genuine interest, she says, but in a spirit of astonishment. He was captivated. “He said, ‘Find out if it’s real,’ and I was like, ‘This is definitely fake.’ But he said, ‘No, find out,’ so I asked our travel agent. And then they came back to us and said, ‘Yeah, it’s possible.’ And I’m like, ‘Really?’” That fateful day scrolling was a turning point of monumental proportions for Dawood. The Instagram reel that she had assumed was computer-generated was in fact genuine footage of the Titan, a submersible that had been constructed to dive to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean, taking tourists to the wreck of the Titanic. And her husband, Shahzada, wanted to go. Everyone knows how the story ends. On June 18, 2023, the Titan imploded off the Titanic’s bow, instantly killing all five on board. Shahzada Dawood was one of them. Their 19-year-old son, Suleman, was at his side. They died alongside fellow tourist Hamish Harding, Paul-Henri Nargeolet, a deep-ocean diver who’d been dozens of times to the Titanic, and Stockton Rush, whose company, OceanGate, had built the Titan — and, it would later emerge, knew about its deficiencies according to the US Coast Guard. Now, after damning reports from the US Coast Guard, the National Transportation Safety Board and its Canadian counterpart about the vessel’s flaws, as well as OceanGate’s “toxic workplace culture” and “intimidation tactics… to evade regulatory scrutiny,” Christine Dawood is ready to talk. Her book, “Ninety-Six Hours: A Wife and Mother’s Desperate Search for the Lost Titan Sub,” was published in May — the result, she says, of “word-vomiting” her pain onto the page. In the three years since the tragedy, Dawood has, she says, dealt with post-traumatic health problems, borne witness to the investigations into OceanGate, and suffered an enraging bureaucratic battle to have the remains of her husband and son returned. A life coach with a psychology degree, she is now channeling her grief into helping others, and plans to open a center for psychosomatic illness and trauma next year in the UK. “I’ve been quiet on purpose, I didn’t want to talk to anybody,” she says. “So why now? I wanted to bring their voices, show the people behind the headlines. They were lovely human beings with their own strengths and weaknesses, their quirks. “I’m slowly starting a new phase with the healing center, and I will never be able to close that chapter, but I think the book rounds it up, and now I can concentrate on the next thing and leave the public behind.” Dawood’s understated memoir starts from the day she met Shahzada, when they were both students in her native Germany, and ends after the prayer ceremony the family held for the dead men in St. John’s, Newfoundland. She recounts in excruciating detail the family’s journey on the Polar Prince — the icebreaker that served as mission control for the Titan’s ill-fated final expedition in the North Atlantic — and the 96 hours she spent after the sub was reported missing, hoping for a positive outcome. She also writes with torturous hindsight about their decision to take the trip. Initially, she was meant to descend to the wreck with Shahzada. She gave her spot to Suleman to gift them a father-son experience to remember. A first glimpse of the Titanic “I wasn’t instantly excited,” she says about that day she saw the Instagram post, speaking in the family home outside London where she still lives with her daughter. Dawood suffers from claustrophobia — even long-haul flights are a trial for her. Her husband did too, she says. But Shahzada was thrilled by the idea of visiting the wreck — and was prepared to battle his claustrophobia to do so — so she volunteered to go with him. “Nature exploration was my thing, like going to a forest or on hikes,” she says. “That was out of his comfort zone but he would have come with me. So I would have gone with him.” Suleman was intrigued, too, but was too young to make the dive when they first saw the ad. In the wake of the catastrophe, much was made of Suleman’s fascination with the Titanic. The 19-year-old had even made a Lego model of the ship — it still sits in the family’s kitchen today. But Dawood says that the Titanic was one of countless interests for Suleman sparked by their family travels. While Harding, the other tourist on the Titan, was a keen adventurer, the Dawoods preferred plusher vacations that taught them something. “We loved a clean toilet and a cushy bed — we were very comfort-oriented,” she says. Shahzada was a history buff, so the family had been to Lebanon to see the ancient Cedars of God forest that the Phoenicians had used to build their ships, becoming the Med’s most famous seafarers. They’d been to England’s Jurassic Coast to hunt for fossils on the beach. They’d seen shipwrecks that had been brought up from the depths in museums. And in 2011, while living in Singapore, they had visited an exhibition about the Titanic, which included objects raised from the wreckage by Nargeolet. “It was something that interested us, like the cedars, or the Parthenon or the Colosseum, or how the Eiffel Tower was built,” she says. The exhibition assigned visitors the name of a real-life Titanic passenger on entry, and revealed at the exit whether that person had survived the tragedy. “It was really well done,” she says. “They had original pieces there: clothes, part of the hull. It was fascinating that it was possible to get all these pieces up, because it’s so deep down.” “In hindsight it looks like that [that Suleman was fascinated] but he also tried to make a painting of Andy Warhol because we went to that exhibition too,” she adds. “He was interested, and he was young. We were like, ‘This is really interesting, and the history and the story is interesting,’ but we weren’t obsessed with it. It was a nice family day. We went for dim sum afterwards.” The drawn-out pandemic meant that Suleman got the chance to take that interest further. By the time travel was allowed, he was old enough to embark on the Titan. The Dawoods’ original plan had been to try a dive of the Hudson Canyon, also offered by OceanGate. “I think they would have been just as happy going down the Hudson,” she says, adding that her family was more interested in the tech that would allow them to dive so deep, rather than the famous wreck in particular. But, emerging from lockdown, they had the same hankering for a bucket-list trip as everyone else. “We decided, OK, let’s go for the big one straightaway.” For the past decade, the family had booked vacations through Quintessentially, a high-end concierge service, says Dawood. When she’d sent them the Instagram video of the Titan, they’d replied offering to arrange it. “They didn’t flag anything — they immediately connected me to them,” she says. “They were very excited — they were on the call with me.” Quintessentially set up an initial call with OceanGate, according to emails seen by CNN. Once the Dawoods paid their deposit, Rush and his wife Wendy, then OceanGate’s communications director, flew over to London to meet them. “I actually saw it as something positive — they’re making an effort, reassuring us,” she says now. Although she dismissed much of Rush’s spiel as “hot air,” she believed the basics. “He was talking about research, which we later found out was complete bullshit,” she says. “He said they are together with NASA, they are doing research with some university, so we thought, OK. None of that was true.” (NASA had consulted with the company over plans for a composite hull, though refused OceanGate permission to use its name in a press release, lest it seem like an endorsement.) Although she trusted her travel concierge to do due diligence on the safety, Dawood did her own research, too. In her book, she describes searching for statistics about submersible accidents and finding nothing. “And I knew Nargeolet would be with us. Somebody who’s been down there 30 times… they called him ‘Mr Titanic.’ Why would I not trust such a person?” In 2025, the US Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation (MBI) report found that OceanGate had failed to analyze hull anomalies following a 2022 dive. It cited the sub’s “inadequate design, certification, maintenance and inspection process” as the primary contributing factors of the disaster, as well as OceanGate’s “toxic workplace culture” and inadequate regulatory framework and whistleblower procedures. The five deaths were “preventable,” it found. In her book, Dawood writes about an investigator telling her not to go down the agonizing road of hindsight. “The head of the investigation said to me, ‘You could not have known,’” she says now. Today, she says, she’d like to see the travel industry more tightly regulated. “If you go to a travel agent, you are placing trust in their expertise,” she says. “That’s their job, right?” She felt that booking through an agent gave more security, she says. Emails reviewed by CNN show Dawood referring to her fear of the planned trip several times when writing to Quintessentially, and the company revisiting the idea of booking the Titanic trip more than once when she had let it go dormant. Quintessentially said in a statement: “Oceangate was widely recognised at the time within the global luxury travel sector. However, Quintessentially did not feature or promote this product on any of its platforms, nor was it proactively recommended to its clients and members or the wider market. At no stage was this Oceangate experience ever proactively marketed or suggested to any client or member.” It emphasized that Dawood was the one who initially mooted the idea and said that its involvement was “limited to providing a professional response to the original request.” A spokesperson added: “Quintessentially is focused on providing the service our clients and members expect of us — whether just to book or otherwise — and we do, of course, alert them to any concerns that arise from our checks.” Slow-burn horror Dawood’s book is a forensic account of her experience on board the Polar Prince, starting from her family’s night-time arrival after a delayed flight to a seemingly abandoned shipyard in St. John’s, Newfoundland — ironically, the trip revolved around the couple’s 21st wedding anniversary and her birthday. Sourced from her journal and from transcripts — she recorded everything after the Titan went missing, she says, in order to report back to relatives on the ground — it’s a slow-burn horror story. At first they laughed, she says, when they realized the ship for this luxury experience was a bare-bones icebreaker, and they’d be sleeping in bunk beds. They weren’t fazed by the unseasonal roughness of the sea, which flung them around as they headed out into the Atlantic, the Titan bouncing along behind them on a raft towed by the Polar Prince. They coped with the nausea, with their plates sliding across the tables as they tried to eat, with the sense of claustrophobia that came from being in the middle of the sea, without a single identifying point in sight. There were two dives planned, with four passengers scheduled — “mission specialists,” as they were called, partly to avoid complying with regulations for passenger vessels, OceanGate co-founder told the US Coast Guard investigation, according to the Washington Post. OceanGate decided that Shahzada, Suleman and Hamish Harding would take the first dive. The second would take a passenger who, in the book, she nicknames JB. After his planned dive partner canceled, JB would be the lucky recipient of a private dive. He would soon find out just how lucky he was. Living hour by hour Christine Dawood and her daughter waved Shahzada and Suleman goodbye at 9 a.m. on June 18, 2023, blowing them a kiss as the sub disappeared underwater. “It was fun,” she says, simply. On the Polar Prince, she recounts in her book, Suleman had admitted that the adventure was far beyond his comfort zone. When she had suggested he didn’t go, he replied that that discomfort was exactly why he wanted to push himself. That morning, he put on his favorite red hoodie and boarded the Zodiac boat that took them to where the Titan and its raft bobbed on the waves. From the Polar Prince, Dawood watched Shahzada joking with Hamish — the pair had become friends. “They were waving at me and smiling and just driving away,” she remembers. “I was happy for them.” Was there any jealousy that she wasn’t going? “Wistfulness,” she says. “I wouldn’t have wanted to have the whole going down and up, but the ‘down there’ would have been nice. I was waiting for them to reach the bottom, then I’d go up to the bridge and live with the experience with them, because we were supposed to get their messages of what they were seeing. Then I would have felt I was seeing it with them.” Tired and seasick, she was having coffee with JB when a woman, who she won’t identify, came into the mess room and announced casually that they’d lost contact with the sub. “I didn’t know what to do with that sentence,” she says. “OK, and now what? It didn’t register.” She went up to the bridge and was reassured that it was “normal.” It took four full days for the crew to acknowledge that something catastrophic had happened to the sub. In the book, Dawood comes across as the person with the most concerns throughout the wait, while OceanGate operatives reassure her. They might be stuck on the seabed or in the wreckage, they suggest. They could have lost contact and been coming up normally. They scan the sea for signs of the Titan bobbing on the surface, and minimize her concerns about dwindling oxygen supplies. They liaise with the coastguard and the flotilla of ships with ROVs (remotely operated vehicles) and other deep-sea equipment that were coming to help. In the meantime they feed her, organize movie screenings, poker games and a “jam session.” Not everyone took part — Dawood kept to herself, and she says that a couple of people on board became “hysterical.” She remained stoical. “I didn’t need to get into crisis as well — I felt, OK, we’ve got this, we have plans on how to get them back up,” she says. “If I’d freaked out that would not help the rescue mission, it would not help the people around me trying to help them, and it would certainly not have helped me.” Instead, she set herself targets of making it through hour by hour, briefing to briefing, meal to meal. “It’s like when you’re on a walk — OK, I’m going to get to that tree and then I’m going to rest. And then at that tree, you’re like, Oh, I still have some energy, I’m going to go to the next tree.” She tried not to think about the darkness down there at the bottom of the ocean. “It’s a different kind of darkness, right? There’s literally no light. Neither Shahzada or Suleman were very good with darkness.” At no point did she think that they might already be dead. She was, she says, in denial. The aftermath On June 22, the US Coast Guard said it had found wreckage on the oceanbed, 1,600 feet from the bow of the Titanic, which lies at a depth of 13,000 feet. The Titan had suffered a catastrophic implosion; the five men had died before their brains had even had time to register what was happening. “It’s the best version of the worst thing that can happen,” says Dawood now. Her voice falters as she remembers her worst fear — that they would be brought to safety, but run out of oxygen on the way up. “If they’d suffocated I would not be where I am today,” she says. What Dawood went through in the aftermath of the tragedy is beyond what many could endure. First there was the media storm — “a juicy story about rich people,” as she calls it. She had to leave the “godforsaken ship,” as she terms the Polar Prince, disguised from the cameras. With her in-laws, she arranged for prayers to be said for Shahzada and Suleman, both Muslims, in St John’s — Islam normally requires a swift burial, though if there’s no body, special prayers can release the souls. She was criticized by some for not seeming emotional enough in the one interview she gave in a bid to curtail media attention. And then she had to come home. “There were no bodies to bring back, all we had was their bags. I put them in Suleman’s room and didn’t look at them for months,” she says. Repatriating their remains — two small boxes of “slush” — became a bureaucratic nightmare. The men had died in international waters, the Polar Prince was Canadian, and the rescue had been US-led. Their remains had been brought to a Canadian port, but the Dawoods lived in the UK. Legally they should have been cremated, but cremation isn’t allowed in Islam. Even with a lawyer, it took nine months. “They had to make sure the DNA was properly separated so that we didn’t get parts from somebody else,” she says. “And then at some point I finally got the message. The flight number. They’re on their way.” The mental trauma caused physical symptoms. She says she developed vertigo, blurred vision, and couldn’t walk in a straight line. She planned to go to the US for the public hearings held by the US Coast Guard’s Marine Board of Investigation in September 2024, but was too unwell to leave the house. Her family doctor, she says, “saved my life many times over.” Eventually, she contacted a private clinic specializing in psychosomatic medicine in Germany. “I guess there is a benefit if things are very public — I wrote that my husband and son died in that accident around midnight, and they called me at 8 a.m. and said, ‘We have a place for you,’” she says, smiling. “And then I just went.” The two months she spent there broke the cycle. Without it, she says, “I might be on a psychiatric ward now.” Her experience is the motivation for her next chapter: launching a similar center in the UK. Due to open by the start of 2028, it will be the country’s first. Moving through grief Three years on, that center is becoming Dawood’s next chapter. “Sometimes I wake up now and that’s the first thought in my mind, not the grief,” she says. “It was quite a profound realization — I can think about something else. I want to help people. I don’t think grief should be experienced alone.” Nargeolet’s family have sued OceanGate, and Dawood says she’s been asked to join lawsuits, but doesn’t want to out of self-preservation. “I don’t want to be consumed by anger,” she says. “I want to be able to look at their pictures and smile.” It’s notable that while she can discuss the details of her relatives’ deaths, she doesn’t mention Stockton Rush by name. She has never heard from OceanGate, she says, not even formal condolences. In the meantime, she takes solace in nature — walking in the Surrey Hills south of London, through a forest of 1,000-year-old yew trees nearby, and feeling connected to Shahzada and Suleman when she’s by the sea. Sometimes she still expects them to walk through the door, she says; if she sees a young man in a red hoodie, she startles, thinking it’s Suleman. Chatting in her home, she occasionally slips into the present tense when talking about them. But through her grief, Dawood is trying to live. She has been on vacation — even to visit friends in Canada. Flying over the North Atlantic was, she says, “very, very uncomfortable.” Writing the book brought out Titanic fans, who came to the signings. Why does she think so many people are intrigued by the story? “Well, it’s a tragedy, isn’t it?” she shrugs. “I think humans are always fascinated by tragedy. “Loss of life in a non-natural way is always a fascination, isn’t it? We’re just programmed to prefer the most gory kinds of stories.”

articles.title: Most Americans think Donald Trump is profiting from presidency unethically or illegally, finds poll
articles.summary: Most Americans believe US President Donald Trump is profiting from his presidency in ways that are either illegal or unethical, while a majority also
articles.body: Most Americans believe US President Donald Trump is profiting from his presidency in ways that are either illegal or unethical, while a majority also think he has prioritised his personal financial interests over helping ordinary people, according to a new poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.The survey found that around six in 10 US adults believe Trump is either illegally profiting from the presidency or engaging in unethical conduct that does not break the law.Around four in 10 believe he is doing something illegal, while about two in 10 think his conduct is unethical but not illegal.Only around two in 10 respondents said Trump was doing nothing wrong, while a similar proportion said they did not know enough to assess the allegations, according to the AP-NORC poll.The findings come as Trump's family business expands into new ventures, including cryptocurrency, following his return to the White House.The poll also found that Americans were more likely to believe Trump had prioritised his own financial interests than the country as a whole or people like them.Majority believe Trump prioritises personal wealthThe survey found that 56% of US adults believe Trump has placed “a lot” of emphasis on his personal businesses since returning to the White House.A similar share, 54%, said he had given the same level of attention to the business interests of his friends and family.By comparison, only around one-quarter of respondents said Trump had prioritised the country as a whole “a lot”, while about one in 10 believed he had given that level of attention to people like them.Barbara Thaxton, an 87-year-old independent voter from Florida, expressed concern about the contrast between Trump's wealth and the financial pressures faced by ordinary Americans.“His wealth increases,” she said, “but the people in the country are just barely getting by.”The White House has repeatedly rejected allegations that Trump and his family are benefiting financially from his position, maintaining that he has no conflicts of interest and acts in the country's interests.Trump, meanwhile, dismissed concerns about conflicts of interest at the beginning of his second term, telling The New York Times that “I found out that nobody cared.”Unlike during his first term, he has lifted a self-imposed restriction on his family pursuing private-sector deals overseas and launched several new cryptocurrency businesses.Financial disclosures, crypto ventures under scrutinyAccording to a federal financial disclosure filed in June, Trump reported receiving more than $1 billion from new cryptocurrency businesses after his administration eased regulations governing the industry,.One of his major crypto ventures received a $500 million investment after his election from a United Arab Emirates business linked to the country's royal family.The venture also received assistance from a cryptocurrency company founded by a Chinese billionaire facing legal trouble in the US.The Trump Organisation has also struck eight foreign real estate deals during the first year of his presidency.Several involved authoritarian or one-party states whose governments have influence over private businesses and have an interest in maintaining favourable relations with Washington.The poll, however, measured public perceptions of Trump's conduct and did not establish whether any of the activities were illegal.Democrats more likely than Republicans to allege wrongdoingPolitical affiliations shaped respondents' views of the allegations. Around eight in 10 Democrats believed Trump was doing something illegal, according to the AP-NORC survey.Independents and Republicans were less likely to believe he had broken the law. Around three in 10 independents and one in 10 Republicans said Trump was doing something illegal. About two in 10 independents and a similar share of Republicans believed his conduct was unethical but not illegal.Most Republicans either believed Trump was doing nothing wrong or said they did not know enough to judge the allegations.Audra Pelsue, a 52-year-old Republican from New York, said she believed Trump's family may have benefited from his position but did not think he had done so personally.“His family has probably benefited, but I don’t think he has,” she said, dismissing his critics as suffering from “Trump derangement syndrome”.Pelsue also questioned what she saw as a double standard in the criticism, pointing to Hunter Biden's position as a director at Ukrainian energy company Burisma while his father, Joe Biden, was vice-president.Americans divided over Trump's prioritiesThe poll found differences among Republicans themselves over how Trump has balanced his personal interests with those of the country. Around half of Republicans said he had placed “a lot” of emphasis on the country, while roughly one-quarter said he had given the same level of attention to his personal business interests. Only around one-quarter believed he had focused “a lot” on people like them.John Bartus, a resident of Idaho, said Trump's decision to donate his presidential salary of USD 400,000 a year was a factor in his assessment of the president's priorities.“It seems like his business interests are a part of his life, but it doesn’t seem like he lets that interfere with what’s going on in the country,” he said. “He puts it on the back burner.”Lisa Fernandez, a 57-year-old Democrat from Texas, offered a contrasting view, accusing Trump of using the presidency to benefit himself and his family.“He's exploiting it for his own needs and his family and making a profit off the people who he is supposed to be serving,” she said. “His whole reason for being is to enrich himself and take what he can take without consequences.”The AP-NORC findings come amid broader dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll last month found his overall approval rating had fallen to 32%, its lowest level in his political career, amid concerns about the cost of living and the war involving Iran.That survey also found that just 17% of respondents approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living, while his overall approval rating had fallen from 35% in the previous week's poll.You use AI every day. articles.title: 11 sailors missing after drone strike sinks merchant vessel near Bulgarian waters
articles.summary: Eleven sailors are missing following a drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian officials, prompting the country’s government to summon the Russian ambassador.
articles.body: Eleven sailors are missing following a drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian officials, prompting the country’s government to summon the Russian ambassador. Overnight there were two attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials said, with one Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship, the “HS Dignity,” being sunk 15 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets – leading to an urgent search and rescue operation. The search for the missing crew members – believed to be Syrian and Egyptian nationals – is still ongoing as of Tuesday afternoon, the Bulgarian Interior Ministry told CNN. Five people in the 16-person crew had already been rescued by other merchant vessels, the ministry said. Another cargo ship called the “Chelsea 3,” which sails under the Maltese flag but is Ukrainian-owned, was struck by three drones as it sailed off the coast of Byala, Bulgaria. Bulgarian border police said they rescued the entire crew of that vessel, which included seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, some of whom were injured in the attack. All were safely transported to the port of Varna, where the injured crew members received medical assistance, authorities said. The country’s president and prime minister both strongly condemned the attacks in the vicinity of Bulgarian waters, which they indicated were likely connected to Russia. “Bulgaria continues to seek support for an investigation into the attacks to determine the country of origin of the drones,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in a social media post on Tuesday. “We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side. However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation,” Radev added. “I will therefore summon the Russian Ambassador for a meeting today.” Russian authorities did not immediately comment on the incidents. CNN has reached out to the Russian Embassy in Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, for comment. Radev added that he informed NATO allies and the European Union of the attacks, as Bulgaria seeks assistance to strengthen air and maritime surveillance and defense. “I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast,” she said. “Those responsible should be held accountable.” “The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable,” European Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen said in a statement, condemning the attack without explicitly mentioning Russia. The latest attacks come after two ships were attacked by marine and aerial drones last week inside Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One of those vessels was damaged and the crew were all rescued, Bulgaria’s prime minister said at the time. A second vessel sank after being attacked and the search operation for the 10-person crew was eventually called off. Attacks in the Black Sea have also heightened fears about global food security, as Ukraine is one of the world’s largest exports of grain. Russia has repeatedly bombed Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, forcing the country to rely on shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO member states Bulgaria and Romania, as well as on Danube river ports. Meanwhile, Ukraine has also stepped up its attacks on Russian grain-exporting ships. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul condemned Tuesday’s strikes on merchant vessels near Bulgaria, calling them “an attack on international shipping & on global food security, depriving the most vulnerable of much-needed supplies” in a post on X. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that the alliance “will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea” and has “already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank.” A CNN analysis of vessels near where the “HS Dignity” was sunk found that a NATO warship belonging to the Bulgarian Navy appears to be assisting in the search and rescue operations. In a statement, the Syrian Seafarers’ Union expressed its “deep concern over the fate of the crew members who are still being searched for.” This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: Pope Leo in the hospital as surgery to remove growth on his lung scheduled for Tuesday
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to the hospital for surgery Tuesday to remove a small growth on his lung, in what is his first stay in hospital since the start of his pontificate.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to the hospital for surgery Tuesday to remove a small growth on his lung, in what is his first stay in hospital since the start of his pontificate. The 71-year-old pontiff told the crowd gathered in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that doctors had discovered a “nodule” on his lung, which he had been advised to have removed. A nodule is a mass of dense tissue that is often benign. Leo said on Sunday that the growth had been detected “at a very early stage” and was “well-contained.” The surgery will take place Tuesday afternoon at the Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic hospital in northwest Rome, a private medical facility that has a long association with the Vatican. The hospital has a special suite of rooms for the pope on the 10th floor, which Pope John Paul II famously dubbed “Vatican three” during his frequent stays there – St. Peter’s being Vatican one and the papal residence Castel Gandolfo, Vatican two. Pope Francis also spent an extended period there early last year when he was treated for pneumonia. The pontiff has cancelled all his public events until October 20. “Surgeries to remove a nodule are usually minimally invasive with a low rate of complications,” said Dr. Matthew Triplette, medical director of the Lung Cancer Screening Program and specialist in pulmonary and critical care medicine. He added that patients normally stay in hospital for a few days and then continue their recovery at home. The Vatican will continue to function while the pope is in hospital although anything requiring his signature will need to be postponed. A spokesman said Sunday that the pope will need about a week to recover following the operation. The Vatican has no specific rules on how the leadership of the Catholic Church is transferred should the pope be incapacitated. Even if he is unconscious and undergoing surgery, the pontiff retains full papal authority. Both Pope Francis and Pope John Paul II issued laws and statements while they were being hospitalized. Day-to-day Vatican operations are already handled by a separate team. Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin told Italian media on Tuesday that Catholic clergy are all praying for the pope’s good health. “We were all struck by the serenity with which the Pope announced this procedure,” Parolin said. “We hope he can resolve this issue as soon as possible. We are confident, but naturally, we are supporting him with our prayers.” Parolin explained that he saw Leo yesterday evening, and that the need for surgery came as a surprise. “We spoke very calmly,” he said. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.” “It is something that, thank God, was detected immediately,” Parolin continued. “And normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.” The pope kept his normal busy schedule Monday, holding back-to-back meetings in the morning before participating in a gathering of bishops and church leaders in the Vatican. News of the first American pope’s surgery has led to an outpouring of well-wishes across the world, including from those visiting Rome. “We’re just hoping that his procedure is going to go well,” said Paul Kavulich, who was visiting Rome on a pilgrimage with his daughter on Monday and is from the pope’s hometown of Chicago. “And he’s got God with him – no doubt about that.” The Vatican press office said the growth on the pope’s lung was discovered during “routine tests.” Leo is not known to have any underlying health problems, and he likes to keep active by playing tennis and going swimming.

articles.title: Storms cause 5 deaths in Mexico as flood risk eases in southwestern U.S.
articles.summary: ENSENADA, México — Hurricane Simon pounded western Mexico with more wind and rain Monday after tropical weather systems caused five deaths and damage in Pacific coastal towns and resorts.
articles.body: ENSENADA, México — Hurricane Simon pounded western Mexico with more wind and rain Monday after tropical weather systems caused five deaths and damage in Pacific coastal towns and resorts. The eye of the Category 2 hurricane remained offshore as its outer bands of winds and rain slammed communities between the Sierra Madre and the Pacific Ocean near Puerto Vallarta. Flood advisories were mostly lifted in the southwestern U.S. after the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel caused weekend flooding in Las Vegas. Hurricane Simon batters Mexico’s Pacific coast In Mexico’s Baja California state, rescuers on Monday combed parts of the coastal city of Ensenada where floodwaters swept away vehicles and damaged homes. At least four people died in the state due to the impact of post-tropical cyclone Rachel. Resident Johana Nuriulu said the flooding began during the night, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity. “We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but really loud,” she said. Nuriulu said she went outside and discovered that a nearby stream had overflowed, sending water rushing through the neighborhood. The waters inundated streets and homes, sweeping away vehicles and other belongings. “Everything was being dragged away” Nuriulu said. Several communities were cut off by landslides and overflowing rivers elsewhere in Baja California. In the afternoon, the Mexican military used helicopters to rescue 32 people — 22 of them foreigners — from a ranch in Ensenada. Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila said 13 were youths. The state Secretary of Security, Gen. Laureano Carrillo, said that some of the group were missionaries meeting at the ranch and that among them were Germans and Americans. Baja California Civil Protection Coordinator Ignacio Lozoya said Monday evening that four bodies had been recovered in Ensenada: a 13-year-old girl on Sunday and two women and a 4-year-old boy Monday. Lozoya said six people remained missing: four in Ensenada and two from the town of San Felipe, a father and son who went fishing Saturday and did not return. According to Ávila some 14,000 federal and state personnel had been deployed across Baja California to assist affected residents and respond to the emergency. To the south, Simon downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal towns of Guerrero state, including the major seaport of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said at a news conference. A 71-year-old man died after a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, Guerrero’s capital, Salgado said. Simon had maximum sustained winds of 155 kph (100 mph) late Monday and was expected to remain a hurricane through midweek, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said Monday evening. It was slowly approaching the western Mexico coast, where heavy rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides before landfall possibly late Friday. In Puerto Vallarta, workers removed wooden panels from boarded-up storefronts and businesses reopened Monday as rains eased. The popular tourist destination’s international airport suspended operations until Tuesday morning. “Personally, I think we should remain on alert because we don’t really know whether it will arrive, move elsewhere or dissipate,” said Noelia Carrillo, a tourism agency worker. Rachel brings flooding to the US Southwest Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved north into Southern California. The storm battered the coast with unusually large waves, which tore apart a boardwalk and smashed into homes in Long Beach. Some residents were forced to evacuate. Las Vegas tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October after receiving 1.08 inches (2.74 centimeters) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the U.S. National Weather Service. The record was set in 1947. Videos posted on social media showed a torrent of water rushing through a street near the Las Vegas Strip, with a Ferris wheel and casinos in the background. Andrew Orrison, a weather service meteorologist, said localized flash flooding was still a risk for the region Monday. “We’ve seen the worst of what Rachel brought ... but unfortunately we are looking at the disturbed weather still lingering,” Orrison said. Flood advisories were mostly lifted by late Monday in Utah, Arizona and elsewhere in the Southwest. In Utah, dozens of runners and volunteers who were part of the Moab 240 ultramarathon were evacuated Sunday after being stranded by flooding. The race goes through Canyonlands and Arches National Park. The additional rainfall is not associated with Rachel, but a different weather system moving across the West, Orrison said. The precipitation is forecast to end by Wednesday. Hurricane Isaias leaves thousands without power in the Southeast Power was gradually being restored after Hurricane Isaias hit the U.S. Southeast. At least four deaths have been linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before dissipating farther north. About 106,000 customers remained without power by Monday evening in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama, according to poweroutage.com. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he expected nearly everyone to have it restored by Tuesday night and directed all schools to reopen Wednesday. Drier weather is expected over the next few days across areas of the mid-Atlantic down through the Southeast, including the southern Appalachians. It will feel “a little summerish” in some of those areas with higher than normal temperatures this week, Orrison said.

articles.title: Morgan Freeman helped revive a historic Mississippi department store by turning it into a blues club hosting hundreds of performances a year, breathing new life into Biloxi’s downtown district
articles.summary: On Howard Avenue in downtown Biloxi, Mississippi, a building that once housed a department store now echoes with blues guitars, clinking glasses and the
articles.body: On Howard Avenue in downtown Biloxi, Mississippi, a building that once housed a department store now echoes with blues guitars, clinking glasses and the murmur of diners settling in for an evening. Ground Zero Blues Club opened here in February 2022, with actor Morgan Freeman among its co-owners. The venue has since expanded into a 20,000-square-foot destination for live music, Southern cooking and private events. Its production manager told the Sun Herald in July 2026 that the club hosts as many as 400 performances a year. The venue has become part of a wider effort to revive Biloxi’s historic commercial district, where vacant storefronts once reflected years of economic decline.How Morgan Freeman helped give Biloxi’s historic Kress Building a second lifeThe building at 814 Howard Avenue was constructed for the S.H. Kress department store in the 1920s. Its brick exterior and decorative façade reflect an era when downtown streets served as important centres of shopping and social life. The Mississippi Department of Archives and History identifies the property as a contributing building in the Biloxi Downtown National Register Historic District. Its records document a fire in November 1942, after which the building was repaired and returned to commercial use.The property later became an entertainment venue known as Kress Live. It operated for roughly two years before closing in 2016, leaving the building without an established business. When Ground Zero moved in, its owners adapted the historic commercial space for live performances, dining and social gatherings while retaining its architectural character.Ground Zero opened in February 2022 following months of renovation. Its design drew inspiration from the original Ground Zero Blues Club in Clarksdale, Mississippi, incorporating concert posters, musical instruments and memorabilia. The renovated space gave the building a new identity while preserving its connection to Biloxi’s commercial history.Morgan Freeman’s long relationship with the bluesFreeman’s involvement in Biloxi grew out of a venture he helped establish more than two decades earlier.In May 2001, the actor opened the original Ground Zero Blues Club in Clarksdale with Bill Luckett and Howard Stovall. Located in the Mississippi Delta, the venue was created to give visitors a place to experience live blues in a region closely associated with the development of the genre.The club’s official history traces its inspiration to local juke joints, where musicians performed in intimate settings for residents and visitors. Ground Zero sought to preserve that atmosphere while giving artists a dedicated stage.Biloxi offered a different setting for the idea. The coastal city has a commercial and cultural identity shaped by tourism, casinos, restaurants and its Gulf Coast location. The new club extended the Ground Zero name to another part of Mississippi.Freeman partnered with New Orleans businessman Eric Meier and brothers Lee and Jeff Young to establish the Biloxi venue. Lee Young was also involved in The District on Howard, a redevelopment project intended to bring businesses and activity back to the historic corridor.Freeman visited the building while renovations were under way. In October 2022, he made an unannounced appearance at the operating club. According to the Sun Herald, patrons were surprised when he came downstairs and took the stage. It was his first visit to experience the completed venue in operation.His involvement brought national attention to the project, connecting the Biloxi venue with his longstanding association with Mississippi blues.Hundreds of performances bring audiences to BiloxiBy July 2026, Ground Zero had developed an extensive live-music programme. Production manager Mick Steele told the Sun Herald that the venue hosts as many as 400 performances annually. Its schedule includes established blues performers and emerging artists from across the country.The programme gives musicians a place to reach audiences in a venue that combines the intimacy of a neighbourhood gathering spot with the facilities of a larger entertainment business. Some visitors arrive specifically for the music, while others come for dinner and stay for a performance.The restaurant broadens the club’s appeal beyond concertgoers. Its menu draws on Southern comfort food, Mississippi Delta traditions and Gulf Coast seafood. Alongside familiar regional dishes, it includes offerings such as boiled peanut hummus.The combination of dining and live music has helped establish the club as a destination throughout the week. In June 2025, the venue expanded into the building’s second and third floors, bringing its reported total area to about 20,000 square feet.The development introduced the Back Room Lounge, featuring a bar and balcony seating, as well as a larger event space for weddings, parties and other private gatherings. The additional floors allow the building to accommodate a wider range of activities, from concerts to celebrations and social events.Local history finds a place above the stageThe Back Room Lounge features historical photographs, murals and memorabilia connected with the Mississippi Gulf Coast. Images associated with Elvis Presley and Biloxi’s entertainment history appear alongside displays celebrating the region’s seafood industry, Mardi Gras traditions and coastal culture.These collections place the club within the broader history of the city. Although blues music remains central to its identity, the displays celebrate the traditions that have shaped the Gulf Coast.The building also holds an unusual feature beneath its floors. During preparations for Ground Zero’s opening in 2022, a trapdoor revealed an underground passage beneath the property. The Sun Herald reported that the tunnel extended towards the middle of Howard Avenue. Biloxi City Attorney Peter Abide said it had once continued in the direction of City Hall on Main Street, although portions had been filled in.The tunnel has fuelled speculation about possible connections to Prohibition-era liquor smuggling, when illegal alcohol sales flourished across the United States. Its discovery added another layer to the history of a building that has served Biloxi through several commercial and entertainment eras.A wider revival along Howard AvenueGround Zero’s opening coincided with renewed efforts to redevelop downtown Biloxi. The club became an anchor business in The District on Howard, a mixed-use project involving historic properties, restaurants, accommodation and other commercial ventures.When the venue opened in 2022, parts of Howard Avenue still had vacant storefronts and properties for sale. By June 2023, a Sun Herald report described a changing district, with properties being sold or renovated and new businesses and accommodation projects emerging along the corridor. Work was also continuing on nearby landmarks, including the Saenger Theatre.Ground Zero provided a regular destination for visitors and demonstrated how a historic commercial property could be adapted for contemporary use. Its concerts brought audiences to Howard Avenue, while the restaurant and event spaces offered additional reasons to visit.The club’s expansion added further activity to the corridor, giving the building a role in the district’s changing commercial landscape. Its presence has coincided with investment in neighbouring properties and efforts to attract new businesses to the area.The redevelopment of Howard Avenue has brought together property owners, developers and city officials working to restore the historic district. Ground Zero has become one of the prominent businesses contributing to that effort, drawing customers into a part of downtown that had struggled to sustain commercial activity.Giving a historic building a futureThe former Kress Building has moved through several identities, from department store to entertainment venue and now to a multi-level blues club and restaurant. Each transformation has given the property a new purpose while retaining its place in Biloxi’s historic commercial district.Freeman’s involvement connected the project to Mississippi’s blues tradition and brought a recognisable public figure to the redevelopment effort. The venue’s programme of concerts, restaurant operations and private events has since established it as a destination for residents and visitors.Today, people enter the old commercial building for live music, Southern food and gatherings. Historical photographs and memorabilia connect the experience to the region’s past, while the stage gives the property a new role in the city’s cultural life.The Kress Building no longer sells department-store goods. Instead, it welcomes musicians, diners and visitors beneath the same historic façade, turning a former retail destination into a gathering place for the blues. Along Howard Avenue, its transformation has become part of Biloxi’s effort to give its historic downtown a new lease on life.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
articles.summary: Activists challenging India’s government over electoral roll controversies have a long legacy of protest to draw on.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital have been flooded in recent days with thousands of armed personnel, chasing down young protesters demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) and struggling to secure a place to stage a sit-in in New Delhi.

Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel.

Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago.

The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup.

But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity.

“Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.”

Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield.

India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration.

For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. But for many of the ancient societies that had agreed to come together under the Indian Union, this led to fears of cultural domination by the Hindi-speaking north of the country.

Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. In January 1965, Annadurai was arrested on the eve of an anti-Hindi agitation. Two young supporters immolated themselves, and Hindi books were burned.

Then-Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri assured protesters that English would continue to be used alongside Hindi. The DMK won Tamil Nadu’s state election in 1967, ending the until-then dominant Congress party’s rule in the state.

It was one of the defining moments of Indian federalism and regional identity in a young nation. English has remained one of India’s two official languages — and the Congress party has never returned to power in Tamil Nadu on its own.

The JP Movement — named after its socialist leader, Jayaprakash Narayan — began amid student protests against corruption, inflation and government mismanagement in the states of Gujarat and Bihar in 1973-74.

Soon, it evolved into a nationwide challenge to then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and her Congress government’s dominance over Indian politics. Students, civil society groups, trade unions and opposition parties subsequently joined the agitation.

Narayan famously called for “Sampoorn Kranti”, or “Total Revolution”, a slogan that still rings in India.

The movement set the stage for a national emergency, declared by Gandhi on June 25, 1975, suspending civil liberties and censoring the press. After the emergency ended, opposition parties united and defeated Congress in the 1977 general election, ending Gandhi’s uninterrupted reign and giving India its first non-Congress government.

The Total Revolution did not come to pass, as Narayan had envisioned, but the movement fundamentally altered opposition politics — showing no leader was beyond the electoral consequences of mass dissent. Many of the leaders who emerged from this movement went on to become state chief ministers and leading federal ministers.

Mandal Commission protests (early 1990s)

In August 1990, then-Prime Minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh announced that his government would implement recommendations of a panel that had been set up more than a decade earlier under a member of parliament, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal. The Mandal Commission, as it was known, recommended that 27 percent of central government jobs be reserved for people from Other Backward Classes (OBCs), communities identified as socially and educationally disadvantaged.

The decision triggered nationwide protests against reservation by students of privileged castes, who feared losing out on their dominance over government jobs. At the time, OBCs only held a little over 12 percent of government jobs — though they represented 52 percent of the national population.

Supporters of reservations argued that concrete actions were needed to address entrenched caste discrimination and unequal access to opportunities.

More than 100 students tried to die by suicide by setting themselves alight, and more than 60 succeeded, during those protests.

In 1992, the Supreme Court upheld the 27 percent OBC reservation in central government employment, excluding the relatively financially better-off “creamy layer” within communities. The move marked one of the largest affirmative action initiatives in independent India.

Protests against liberalisation, globalisation (early 1990s)

Rather than a unified campaign, the protests arose from a series of labour protests and strikes against India’s economic reforms, launched in 1991 under then-Prime Minister PV Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, who would go on to become prime minister in 2004.

The reforms reduced restrictions on private enterprise and opened more sectors to foreign investment. Trade unions feared that privatisation and easier business closures would cause job losses, weaken collective bargaining and erode workers’ protections.

Left-aligned political parties supported many of these protests. But the protests could not prevent the reform programme from proceeding.

Successive governments have continued to expand private sector participation, pursue disinvestment in state-owned enterprises, and modify labour regulations.

Anna Hazare’s anticorruption movement (2011)

The movement erupted amid public anger over major corruption scandals involving the Congress-led coalition government, including a controversy around licensing of the country’s 2G spectrum and allegations surrounding preparations for the 2010 Commonwealth Games, held in New Delhi.

Activists demanded a strong law with an independent anticorruption ombudsman empowered to investigate and punish corruption involving public officials.

Social activist Anna Hazare led the movement through hunger strikes, also featuring activists such as Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi and Prashant Bhushan. Its demonstrations attracted large crowds across the country.

Parliament passed a law in December 2013, establishing a statutory framework for an anticorruption watchdog. But more than a decade later, its impact is minimal.

The movement was divided over whether activists should enter electoral politics. Kejriwal broke away to establish the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in 2012 and went on to become a two-time chief minister of Delhi state.

The legacy of the movement remains largely in the shadow of Kejriwal today, who is now in opposition after Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won the Delhi state election last year.

Protests following the ‘Nirbhaya’ gang rape (2012)

On December 16, 2012, a 23-year-old paramedical student was gang-raped and brutally assaulted on a moving bus in New Delhi. She died on December 29 while receiving treatment. Victims of sexual assault cannot be named publicly under Indian law. So she was widely referred to as “Nirbhaya”, meaning fearless in Hindi.

The crime triggered mass demonstrations against sexual violence, unsafe public spaces, inadequate policing and the treatment of women in the country. Protesters demanded justice for the victim and fundamental changes to how authorities handled sexual assault cases.

Students, young people, women’s rights activists, and common residents mobilised in Delhi, including around India Gate and other key locations.

Four adult defendants were convicted and sentenced to death; their executions took place in 2020.

Parliament passed the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, broadening the legal recognition of sexual offences, criminalising offences including stalking and voyeurism, and strengthening penalties for several crimes.

Activists continue to argue that stronger laws alone cannot address entrenched misogyny and inadequate policing. And crimes against women, including sexual crimes, remain rampant across most parts of India, including the capital.

India’s Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), passed in December 2019, offers an expedited path to Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who arrived before December 31, 2014. Muslims were excluded from this provision.

Critics argued that making religious identity a basis for preferential citizenship undermined India’s secular constitutional principles. Millions feared the law could work alongside a proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) to place Muslims at greater risk of exclusion and possible expulsion from India.

The movement was decentralised. Students at Jamia Millia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University led major demonstrations, while women-led sit-ins, especially at Shaheen Bagh in Delhi, became national symbols of resistance against Prime Minister Modi’s Hindu majoritarian politics.

In February 2020, large-scale mob violence primarily targeting Muslims broke out in northeastern Delhi. More than 50 people, mostly Muslims, were killed.

Meanwhile, the sit-in in Shaheen Bagh lasted 101 days before police cleared the site on March 24, 2020, soon after imposing the COVID-19 lockdown. Dozens of Muslim activists were arrested and charged under antiterrorism laws. Student leaders such as Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam remain in jail, six years on, with no trial.

The protests could not secure repeal of the law, but delayed its implementation. The government notified its implementation in March 2024, bringing the citizenship process into operation.

In 2020, the Modi government introduced three agricultural laws intended to liberalise farm markets and facilitate direct sales to private buyers.

Many farmers, particularly in northern India, feared that the changes would weaken the government-regulated wholesale markets through which much of their produce was sold. They also worried that the reforms would undermine the minimum support price (MSP), a government-set price for certain crops.

Numerous farmer unions surrounded and shut down roads leading up to Delhi under the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, a coalition formed to coordinate the agitation. Thousands of farmers camped on Delhi’s outskirts for months.

More than 700 farmers died amid extreme weather, road accidents, suicides and clashes.

In November 2021, Modi announced that the government would repeal the laws.

It marked the first such moment when protesters had wrestled a significant concession from Modi, who built his political currency as a leader who does not compromise.

It was a dig at India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant’s remarks, equating the country’s unemployed youth with “cockroaches” and “parasites”, sparking fury in the backdrop of a decade of sliding in multiple democratic indices.

Student Abhijeet Dipke doubled down on the viral joke, creating a pressure group – the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – and led protests against irregularities in the national medical school entrance examination. The newbie protesters of the CJP movement were held together by left student organisations, choking Parliament Street and the popular protest site Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.

The Gen Z protests eventually forced out the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, in July 2026.

The CJP protesters have again come together, along with opposition parties, this time demanding CEC Kumar’s resignation.

articles.title: Trump to campaign in Ohio, Alaska to help Republicans retain control of Congress in US midterms
articles.summary: With just over three weeks left before the US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump is stepping up campaign rallies across Republican-friendly
articles.body: With just over three weeks left before the US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump is stepping up campaign rallies across Republican-friendly states to boost candidates facing tight races.According to news agency Reuters, Trump's campaign swing this week includes Ohio, Alaska, Arizona and Montana, all states he won in the 2024 presidential election. Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress as they face headwinds from high gasoline prices and the ongoing war in Iran.The November 3 elections will determine whether Republicans can hold on to their congressional majorities for the final two years of Trump's presidency.Trump is expected to have campaigned in 11 states over two weeks by the end of this week. His schedule includes two stops each in Texas and Ohio, along with a rally in Alaska on Tuesday. Republicans are hoping his visits will help candidates in competitive Senate races.In Ohio, Trump is campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who faces a close contest against Democrat Sherrod Brown. In Alaska, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is also fighting a tight race against Democrat Mary Peltola.Trump said on Saturday that he wanted to thank voters in states that had consistently supported him, while acknowledging that some of those states had closely contested races.Larry Sabato, director of the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, said Trump's campaign stops appeared strategically planned to draw supportive crowds and help Republican candidates.“His staff is putting him in places where he's likely to be able to draw a friendly crowd to the rally,” Sabato said, according to Reuters.However, Trump's rallies have also energised his opponents. Marilyn Makiewicz, a 59-year-old Democratic voter who attended a protest outside a recent rally in Vandalia, Ohio, said she believed Trump was holding the events because he was concerned about the election.White House officials said the campaign stops were aimed at mobilising Trump's loyal supporters and encouraging them to vote. Trump has repeatedly urged his followers to act as though he himself were on the ballot.“Some of them may not show up for a candidate unless Trump gives them a reason,” a White House official said of the president's supporters, Reuters reported.You use AI every day.
