articles.title: BBC FM radio transmissions suspended in Afghanistan
articles.summary: BBC programming is still reaching audiences on shortwave, medium wave, via satellite and online.
articles.body:
Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country.

A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate.

The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022.

"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement.

The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite".

It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools.

Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country."

The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country.

Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men.

People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers.

The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.

articles.title: A student launched an eyelash-serum brand from her mother's kitchen and generated more than £100,000 during one 12-hour livestream
articles.summary: Daisy Kelly launched her beauty brand, Glow For It, from her mother's kitchen table in 2020 while she was still a student.
articles.body: Daisy Kelly launched her beauty brand, Glow For It, from her mother's kitchen table in 2020 while she was still a student. The business, which began after Kelly developed an eyelash serum inspired by her own experience of pulling out her eyelashes, now generates £6 million a year in sales. More than 40% of its sales come through TikTok Shop UK, where livestream shopping has become a major sales channel. Kelly told the BBC that the brand generated more than £100,000 in revenue during a single 12-hour TikTok livestream, describing the format as a turning point for her business.How did TikTok live shopping change Glow For It's business growthKelly told the BBC that a single 12-hour TikTok livestream generated more than £100,000 in revenue for Glow For It. She said the format had significantly affected the company's growth, describing the experience as a direct way to connect with customers and respond to their questions."I think live shopping gives people that connection and interaction that we're all craving," Kelly said. She added that the livestream's performance had changed the direction of her business, saying, "It's categorically changed the trajectory of my business."The company broadcasts from a studio for a minimum of six hours a day, using different presenters to demonstrate its products and interact with shoppers. The sessions include product demonstrations and responses to customer queries, allowing potential buyers to learn more about the items while watching the stream.Kelly compared the experience to operating a physical retail outlet, saying, "It's like having 500 people in your shop." Her experience illustrates how livestreams have become an important part of Glow For It's sales operation, alongside its other TikTok Shop activity.How is livestream shopping changing the online retail industryGlow For It's experience comes as livestream shopping expands across online retail platforms. According to the BBC, services offering livestream shopping include Instagram Live, YouTube Shopping, eBay and Amazon Live, although the formats differ between platforms.Research from retail agency Savvy Marketing found that 30% of shoppers surveyed had purchased something through a live shopping event. Catherine Shuttleworth, the agency's chief executive, said retailers needed to develop a strategy for the format as it continued to grow.TikTok Shop reported that its UK sales increased by more than 30% year on year in June 2026. The platform also said livestream shopping was its fastest-growing format, with more than 6,000 livestreams taking place each day.The figures provide context for the channel's role in Glow For It's business. For Kelly, livestreams have become a significant part of the company's sales activity, with the brand using regular broadcasts to demonstrate products and communicate directly with potential customers.How are small businesses using TikTok Shop livestreams to increase salesManny Malik, a halal butcher from Wolverhampton, uses TikTok Shop to sell meat from his family business, Malik Butchers. Malik said a three-hour TikTok livestream had generated £8,000 in meat sales the previous week. He explained that selling the same amount would normally take three to four days through the family shop.Malik said the platform had helped support the business's expansion, with a second store planned in Stoke. However, he also highlighted the commission charged by online marketplaces. TikTok Shop UK keeps up to 9p from every £1 sold under its standard commission structure.Another example was Buket Sevik, founder of jewellery brand Adorina. After leaving her business manager job to establish the company in February 2026, she began selling through TikTok Shop in May. She told the BBC that the business had grown from 50 orders a month to 500 orders a week after she started livestream selling.Sevik said livestreaming offered flexibility because she could choose when to broadcast around her responsibilities as a mother. Demand had increased to the point where she was trying to hire someone to help with the business.Why are Gen Z and Gen Y shoppers more likely to buy viral productsThe growth of livestream shopping has also raised concerns about consumer spending. articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins French teens on new day of school protests
articles.summary: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined a demonstration outside a high school in a working-class suburb of Paris on Tuesday as French pupils took to the streets for another day of protests over poor conditions.
articles.body: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined a demonstration outside a high school in a working-class suburb of Paris on Tuesday as French pupils took to the streets for another day of protests over poor conditions. Now in its fourth week, the nationwide movement to highlight teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and the dilapidation of facilities has involved marches, blockades of hundreds of schools and, in some cases, clashes with police. Pupils clustered outside the doors of several schools in Paris and other cities in the morning hours, brandishing placards and megaphones and chanting slogans, and marches were planned later in the day. Education Minister Edouard Geffray told France Inter radio that about 200 schools were closed, although he suggested some of the closures were due to safety precautions as they were on the routes of planned marches. Thunberg, who rose to fame as a teenage protester against climate change but has since broadened her activism, said the French pupils deserved wider support. “They should know that all over the world we are following these developments. We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights,” she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction. “Whether it’s not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises ... it’s about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future.” Thunberg also criticized the police response, which has been fiercely debated, as an “extremely violent” sign that authorities were protecting the status quo and ignoring young people’s demands. Riot police have used tear gas and charged at protesters in numerous incidents, injuring hundreds and arresting thousands. The government suspended the use of stun grenades last week after one teenager lost a hand. While left-wing politicians have criticized the police, far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen and others have blamed violent protesters and highlighted damage inflicted on schools and injuries to staff and police officers. The protest movement has added to a sense of uncertainty and crisis engulfing France six months ahead of a presidential election that could usher in the first far-right government since World War Two, led by Le Pen’s National Rally. The cash-strapped government has promised to act to address the pupils’ concerns, but has little room for maneuver at a time when concerns over the national debt and the budget deficit are pushing up borrowing costs to the highest level in years. Le Pen, the frontrunner to replace President Emmanuel Macron according to opinion polls, has said she would slash spending to bring public finances under control.

articles.title: Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting
articles.summary: Hundreds of people have gone missing in Yemen, with families not knowing whether they were killed in fighting or detained.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – In 2020, 18-year-old Munif bid farewell to his family and left his home in Sanaa to fight with the Houthis on the front lines of Yemen’s civil war

After six months, all of his comrades went back to their families, but Munif never returned home.

More than six years have passed, and Munif’s family, who asked to use just his first name for security reasons, are still searching for answers about his fate.

He is one of hundreds of people who have disappeared in Yemen since war broke out in September 2014, when the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – captured the capital and forced the internationally-recognised government to flee south.

“Ten other men from our village joined the front line on the Saudi-Yemen border. All of them came back. We asked them about my brother’s whereabouts, but none could tell us where he had gone,” said Mohammed, Munif’s brother. “A definite answer about his status would be a relief for the entire family.”

There were hopes that a truce in 2022 between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and Iran-aligned Houthis could help families begin their search for their missing loved ones.

Since July this year, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has received more than 1,800 tracing requests from families looking for missing relatives in Yemen.

But the resumption of fighting in July has halted this search for many families, who are trying to find out if loved ones have been detained, injured, killed, or simply lost in records, due to displacement or desertion.

After careful consideration, Mohammed believes there are two possible outcomes for his brother, Munif.

“He might have been hit by an air strike, leaving no trace of his body, or perhaps he was captured, and he remains in captivity,” Mohammed said.

If Munif was killed in an explosion, finding a body part that could be identified would bring the family some relief. But the family is still hoping for the latter scenario, and that Munif is being held captive by government forces.

“We would have accepted his death, adjusted to the loss, and forgotten my brother’s possible return. We just need to know what happened to him,” he said.

“We have heard about some fighters who were believed to be dead, and their families accepted the news of their deaths and mourned them. However, they emerged alive after years of captivity. So, Munif may still be alive.”

Both sides have held many prisoners of war over the decade-long conflict, but the number of captives remains uncertain.

In May, Yemen’s internationally-recognised government and the Houthis signed a United Nations-backed agreement in Jordan to exchange more than 1,600 detainees. However, the implementation of the deal was postponed after both sides accused each other of obstructing the agreement.

Abdulaziz, 24, has been on the front lines in Marib, an energy-rich region in central Yemen, fighting for the Houthis. Before the recent surge in fighting, he used to call his family once every 10 days. But for the past two months, his family has not heard from him.

“We are waiting for a phone call from Abdulaziz, and we do not know if he will ever call us,” said Ahmed, Abdulaziz’s brother.

Fighting has intensified on the front lines in Marib and Al-Jawf since the Houthis seized part of the Yemeni coast in September, and Rashid al-Alimi, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a counteroffensive by government forces.

The use of artillery, drones and warplanes to target Houthi positions likely means that many more people will be killed or missing.

Ahmed, 26, assumes that his brother may have been killed in attacks by government forces in recent weeks.

“We have not received any information from his comrades and field leaders about his injury or death. But my parents state that Abdulaziz’s voice or appearance is the only believable proof that he is alive,” he said.

“Abdulaziz is in the battlefield. And people there kill or get killed. So, his [possible] death is not a shock for me. But continued ambiguity is more painful than confirmed news of his death.”

With no word on his whereabouts, Abdulaziz’s mother will not know whether to wait for his safe return or begin to mourn his loss. “Whether he continues to be lost or his dead body returns, my mother’s eyes will never stop filling with tears,” Ahmed added.

Christine Cipolla, the head of the ICRC’s Yemen delegation, said families of the missing had the right to know about the fate of their loved ones.

“Behind every missing person is a family living in anguish. Their pain cannot be ignored, and their wait must not be prolonged,” she said in a statement .

Two months ago, Ali, 23, joined the Houthis’ campaign against government forces on Yemen’s western coast.

His parents objected to Ali leaving home to fight. But because he was unemployed, he insisted on joining the Houthis.

Five days ago, the family received a call informing them of Ali’s death.

“We were told that Ali was killed in the fighting in Mocha. So far, we have not received his body, and we do not know where it is,” Yasser told Al Jazeera. “Recovering his corpse would ease our grief, end our uncertainty, and prove that he is really dead.”

Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the ICRC and other qualified humanitarian teams must be allowed safe access to all parts of Yemen to recover bodies, document the missing and preserve identification evidence.

“This is not only about meeting legal obligations. Families may carry the pain and uncertainty of not knowing for decades, and their experiences will become part of how this war is remembered,” Al-Jeddawy said.

Some missing people may have been detained or forcibly disappeared, while others may have been killed in fighting or separated from their families.

The Yemen-based NGO, Mwatana for Human Rights, conducted more than 2,000 interviews with families of victims between September 2014 and July 2025. The study reported at least 1,592 incidents of enforced disappearance involving 2,120 victims.

The Houthi armed group was found responsible for 756 incidents of disappearance involving 897 victims. Forces linked to the internationally-recognised government were connected to 351 incidents involving 449 victims, while the Saudi-led Arab coalition was responsible for 65 incidents involving 91 victims. Forces linked to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) were involved in 387 incidents involving 630 victims.

Al-Jeddawy said the issue of the missing is another stain on both sides of the conflict, which has already killed between 150,000 and 227,000 people and displaced millions.

“History will judge the parties not only by the battles they fought or the territory they gained, but also by whether they showed basic humanity towards the dead, the missing and the families left searching for answers,” he said.

articles.title: Mexican gang kidnaps officials to force detained member's release
articles.summary: The gang seized the officials shortly after a high-ranking member was detained, demanding he be released.
articles.body:
A Mexican gang seized three officials in the central state of Morelos on Monday in order to force authorities to release one of the gang's high-ranking members, who had been detained hours earlier.

The attorney-general's office in Morelos said it had arrested a member of the Pueblos Unidos criminal gang, after carrying out a raid as part of its fight against extortion.

Pueblos Unidos retaliated by capturing three people employed by the attorney-general's office and holding them hostage.

In a statement, the office said that it released the detained suspect in order to safeguard the lives of its staff, but stressed that the kidnapping of its employees would not go unpunished.

The gang released all three employees on Monday evening local time, the statement added. One was taken to hospital with a gunshot wound but was in a stable condition.

The decision to release the detained gang member followed official guidelines, which say the lives of kidnap victims have to be put first, according to the statement.

Criminal gangs in Mexico often unleash a wave of violence in an attempt to force a release after one of their leaders is arrested.

In 2019, hundreds of gunmen from the Sinaloa cartel flooded into the city of Culiacán in northern Mexico following the arrest of Ovidio Guzmán, the son of the cartel's infamous founder, Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán.

They erected burning roadblocks and engaged in deadly gunfights with security forces.

The violence was such that the president at the time, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, personally ordered the release of Ovidio Guzmán .

López Obrador said that he had given the order "so as not to put the population at risk".

"The capture of a criminal is not worth more than people's lives," he added.

Guzmán was recaptured in 2023 and extradited to the United States.

More recently, the killing of one Mexico's most wanted criminals, Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera, in February of this year triggered retaliatory attacks from his cartel in 20 Mexican states.

President Claudia Sheinbaum deployed thousands of soldiers to the states affected to quell the violence.

articles.title: Potentially paralysed tourist stranded in Greece after balcony fall
articles.summary: Denby McLaren has a broken vertebra and multiple fractures to her foot
articles.body:
A Scottish tourist who fell from a balcony in Greece is unable to travel home due to the cost of a specialist flight.

Denby McLaren from Larkhall cannot currently use her legs after the three-storey fall, which happened while she was visiting Rhodes to celebrate her 30th birthday.

She has a broken vertebra and multiple fractures to her foot, with her family now waiting to learn if she has suffered permanent injuries.

An air ambulance offering stretcher and medical assistance is needed to get back to Scotland, but these are not covered by her travel insurance. A fundraiser has now been set up to help.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Denby, who works as cabin crew with an airline, was on holiday with her mum Sharon when the accident happened on 6 October.

She has been in hospital since then, with her partner Craig Anderson travelling to Greece to be with her.

Leeanne Weir, a friend of the family, told BBC Scotland News: "It's absolutely horrific. She can't move her legs, she has a broken vertebra and multiple broken bones.

"The biggest worry is that she can't move her legs and we don't know whether this has affected her spine and if she will be paralysed. But she is also lucky to be alive after a fall like that.

"Denby is a lovely girl, just a really sweet person. It's awful what's happened to her."

Although Denby has medical cover, it does not extend to paying for the specialist repatriation needed.

Leeanne said: "The worry is also that the longer she is there in Greece all the other bills are going up for every extra day they are there.

"Apart from the severity of the injuries they have the language barrier and the added pressure of just trying to get home."

The Go Fund Me page has so far raised about £19,000 of the £28,000 target.

Leeanne said: "It doesn't have to be a huge contribution - we have had a phenomenal response from people so far, whether it's £5 or £50.

"We just want to get her home and start being cared for at home."

articles.title: Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
articles.summary: Iran has warned that cables and data centres in the region could be attacked, as Houthi allies hold internet chokepoint.
articles.body:
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.

The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. Fierce fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.

Data centres and US business interests were hit in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates during the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran said these attacks were in response to US attacks on Iranian civilian installations.

Active hostilities have largely ended since the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but attacks on ships passing through the global oil chokepoint – the Strait of Hormuz – have continued.

So how exposed is the region’s internet? Here’s what you need to know:

Why are data centres and internet cables vulnerable?

Because so much data travels through a few narrow routes.

More than 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, according to estimates by the research firm TeleGeography.

They enter the sea through Bab al-Mandeb, a strait about 26km (16 miles) wide at its narrowest, one of the busiest maritime routes connecting Europe to Asia.

Cables can be cut by anchors or sabotage, and repairs in a war zone need permits and safety guarantees.

Data centres, which run banking apps and cloud services, are large, fixed targets.

“An attack does not necessarily need to destroy the servers themselves to render an entire facility inoperable,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

Data centres depend on uninterrupted electricity, cooling and telecommunications, he said, while undersea cables “are difficult to protect continuously and disruption can affect several countries simultaneously”.

Has Iran threatened to attack data centres and cables?

Yes, repeatedly since the war began in February.

On March 11, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a list of “Iran’s new targets”, including cloud infrastructure belonging to Google, Microsoft and Oracle in Israel and some Gulf states.

That same month, the IRGC named 17 US firms in a Telegram post, including Google, Meta, and Apple, as well as the Emirati AI company G42 as potential targets.

Krieg said he would take Rezaei’s threat seriously, but drew a distinction between Iran’s ability to cause significant disruption and its ability “to systematically destroy the Gulf’s digital infrastructure”.

“What makes Mohsen Rezaei’s warning particularly significant is that he is not simply threatening another set of targets,” he said. “He is identifying a new category of strategic infrastructure that connects Gulf economic diversification directly to American technological power.”

He described the warning as “fundamentally about deterrence”, aimed “as much at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha as at Washington”, giving Gulf governments a reason to discourage another US offensive.

Have tech infrastructure and cables been attacked before?

In March, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said two of its facilities in the UAE were “directly struck” by drones, while a strike near one in Bahrain “caused physical impact to our infrastructure”.

Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank said its app was unavailable due to a region-wide IT disruption, though it did not directly link this to AWS.

In September, AWS said it could not restore several sites in Bahrain and one in the UAE.

Under the sea, three cables were damaged in February 2024, most likely by the dragging anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship disabled by a Houthi missile, according to the industry consensus reported by Data Center Dynamics, with repairs taking months.

In September 2025, two cables were cut near Jeddah, slowing internet access across the Middle East and South Asia. No cause has been confirmed.

The March attacks “exposed the limits of treating commercial infrastructure as something that automatically benefits from national air defence”, Krieg said.

“Gulf militaries can intercept most incoming threats, but even a small number of successful strikes can produce disproportionate economic consequences,” he said, adding that relatively cheap drones can threaten facilities holding billions of dollars’ worth of equipment.

Have the Houthis attacked undersea cables?

Not directly, as far as is known, and the group has denied causing the 2024 damage.

But in mid-September, the Houthis seized the port of Mocha and territory around Bab al-Mandeb.

On September 11, they reached Mayyun Island, which splits the strait in two.

On October 5, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it had retaken Mocha and positions near the strait. The Houthis denied it.

Some, but they cost more and are still being built.

On September 10, Iraq signed a contract with Qatar’s Ooredoo to carry data from the Gulf to Europe across its territory, the Ministry of Communications said in a statement.

Minister Mustafa Jabar Sanad told the Iraqi News Agency the underground cable runs from al-Faw to Rabia near Turkiye’s border.

On October 7, Ooredoo’s international arm agreed to buy fibre from Iraq’s iQ Networks to extend the route towards Turkiye, subject to government approval.

Microsoft said in September it would invest more than $400m in subsea and land connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, in a blog post.

The technology news site Rest of World reported on October 7, citing an unnamed source, that Google and Meta had begun sending some traffic through Iraq.

Neither company has responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Krieg said genuine resilience would require geographical redundancy, “potentially including facilities outside the Gulf”.

“That creates a tension between digital sovereignty and operational security,” he said, as Gulf governments have invested heavily in keeping sensitive data and computing within their own borders.

How will it affect the Gulf’s tech hub ambitions?

Investment continues, but the war has already taken a toll on the sector. Gulf states have staked their post-oil economies on technology.

In Abu Dhabi, the Emirati firm G42 is building Stargate UAE with OpenAI, Nvidia and others.

It sits within a planned 5-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus.

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund launched Humain, an AI company chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in May 2025 to build data centres and an Arabic-language AI model, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund joined the US investor Blue Owl in a $3bn data centre push in September 2025.

In September, Microsoft said it would invest more than $10bn in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through 2030, with a new focus on “digital resilience”, in a blog post.

But AWS said it had “exhausted every option” to restore some data hosted in Bahrain.

Krieg said the threats would not “fundamentally reverse” Gulf ambitions, but would “change the economics and geography of AI investment”.

“The Gulf has traditionally sold itself as a stable environment in an unstable region. The war has challenged that proposition,” he said.

The UAE is particularly exposed, he said, because its AI strategy is “deeply integrated with American technology companies”, making Emirati infrastructure “more attractive as a target for Iran”. Qatar, with its diplomatic ties to Tehran, is “somewhat better positioned politically”.

“In many ways, Iran is threatening to do to the Gulf’s emerging digital economy what it has already done to its maritime economy,” Krieg said – to “make reliability itself a geopolitical bargaining chip”.

articles.title: Hungarian parliament scraps Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures
articles.summary: LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but call for changes to other Orbán-era laws.
articles.body:
The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other Orbán-era laws.

The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism".

Since Orbán's April election defeat, the Tisza government of Péter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy.

Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release €4.2bn (£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government.

The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds and readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.

Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly.

Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that Orbán's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation.

"We are very happy that this got adopted," Tamás Dombos of civil rights group the Háttér Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed."

Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image.

But while Fidesz under Viktor Orbán appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister Péter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality.

In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to his supporters that he would prevent it happening.

Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions.

The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in Orbán's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss.

In his own election campaign, Péter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters.

"We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side."

This marked a major improvement on the Orbán years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents.

"I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities."

Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday.

"There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website.

articles.title: The coolest temperatures since spring are finally on the way. See how far they will drop
articles.summary: Fall weather is finally coming to much of the United States.
articles.body: The atmosphere’s attempts to make it feel actually like fall across much of the United States have been repeatedly thwarted in recent weeks, but that’s about to change in a major way. Temperatures will plummet to their lowest levels since spring for many east of the Rockies later this week as a potent cold front slices across the country. The dramatic pattern flip won’t come a moment too soon for some still roasting under summerlike heat: Dozens of locations in the central and southern US will soar to record high temperatures on Tuesday, but the incoming front will drag those highs down by more than 30 degrees in many locales by Friday or Saturday. Some spots in the northern US this weekend could flirt with freezing temperatures overnight for the first time since spring, too. The cold front could also ramp up a multi-day flood threat in the Plains and Texas. When temperatures will drop Things will have to get worse before they get better. Summerlike heat will peak Tuesday in the central US, with highs in the 90s forecast as far north as Illinois and Indiana, and 80s through the Ohio Valley. St. Louis could experience its hottest day this late into the year when it soars into the mid-90s Tuesday. Detroit and Cleveland are forecast to top out in the 80s and could break their high temperature records for the date. The heat will ease only slightly on Wednesday as the front starts to impinge on the central US, but the South will continue to swelter under widespread temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s. Atlanta could challenge its record high for the date of 87 degrees Fahrenheit on Wednesday. The same goes for Nashville’s record of 89 degrees Fahrenheit. Thursday will be another hot day for the Southeast and south-central US, but the big temperature swings will begin in the Plains and parts of the Upper Midwest as the cold front continues its slow journey east. Kansas City, Missouri, could max out in the mid 70s on Thursday after topping 90 degrees Fahrenheit Tuesday — a nearly 20-degree reversal. The turnaround kicks in even more Friday, when highs in the 50s and 60s are forecast from the Plains to the Midwest and Ohio Valley. St. Louis may only reach the low 60s — more than 30 degrees cooler than Tuesday’s likely record-breaking temperature. That would also mark the city’s coolest day since early May. Chicago is in the same boat: Its high temperature is also expected to be nearly 30 degrees cooler than Tuesday and its forecast high in the lower 50s would mark the chilliest day since early May. Fall finally comes for all of the East Coast and South on Saturday as the front reaches the coast. Highs in the 60s and 70s are expected in the South, while the Great Lakes and Northeast only top out in the 50s or 40s. New York City could barely hit the low 50s on Saturday, meaning it’ll likely be the coolest day since late April. Washington, DC, will also have its coldest day since late April, with its high expected to max out in the mid-50s. Atlanta will peak in the upper 60s. That would have marked the coolest day since early May if not for the rainy, windy and cool day former Hurricane Isaias created last Saturday. But the city will definitely hit its coldest overnight low since spring by early Sunday morning, when the temperature dips below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Sunday will also mark the coldest morning since spring in Nashville, Dallas, New York City, Washington, DC, and many other locations. The cooldown won’t be very long-lived as unseasonable warmth is likely to return next week. Flood potential The coming fall weather will bring a streak of danger to the central US midweek. Deep tropical moisture flowing from the Gulf will slam against the cold front when it’s draped over the Plains and fuel a multi-day flood threat. Storms could also train, or move repeatedly move over the same areas like train cars on a railroad track. Wednesday and Thursday are the days with the most flood concern, but some issues could begin as early as Tuesday evening. Scattered severe thunderstorms could also fire up near the cold front late Tuesday afternoon or in the early evening. Damaging winds and hail will be the main threats, but an isolated tornado is possible. The areas most at risk of flooding are also still dealing with serious drought conditions. The rain is much-needed, but flash flooding is possible if it falls faster than the dry ground can absorb. The flood risk will diminish Friday as the front starts to move east.

articles.title: University of Maryland club tennis team suspended after sharing racist imagery
articles.summary: The University of Maryland club tennis team has been suspended indefinitely after it included a racist graphic in a weekend tournament program in College Park, the school said in a statement.
articles.body: The University of Maryland club tennis team has been suspended indefinitely after it included a racist graphic in a weekend tournament program in College Park, the school said in a statement. According to the statement from UMD Recreation and Wellness, the school learned that the team handed out materials with “a graphic containing racist imagery targeting people who are Black or African American.” “They emailed this information to other university tennis clubs in the region about this weekend’s fall tournament at College Park,” the statement said. The UMD statement noted that the incident may have involved only a few team members but that the school still chose to suspend the entire team until the Office of Student Conduct completes its investigation. The matter has also been referred to the University of Maryland Police Department, the school said. The police department confirmed that it is conducting an investigation but declined to provide more information. The UMD Office of Student Conduct did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “The University of Maryland is horrified and expresses its regret and sincere apology for the harm that this has caused,” the school said in the statement. The tennis team forfeited its matches in the tournament, which continued for all other participating teams. Leaders of the UMD club tennis team apologized to other team captains and took responsibility for sending the racist graphics, the statement said. Each invited team also received an apology email from the UMD tennis team. UMD was on-site to support the visiting teams and sent an apology email to the recreation directors at the affected schools, as well as the presidents of the participating teams. One of those presidents was Toni Rachal, who represents the club tennis team at Howard University, a historically Black school. In a statement posted to its Instagram account, the Howard team said Rachal noticed the graphic in a shared Google Doc emailed to participating teams. The graphic contained “a recognizable symbol associated with the Ku Klux Klan (KKK) on the first page” below the UMD club tennis logo, the statement said. “KKK pointed hood masks complete with eye holes appear in the top right and lower left quadrants, replacing the Crossland coat of arms of the official Maryland state flag,” the statement described. “The imagery is a recognizable symbol of white supremacy, organized hate, and violence.” Members of Howard’s team said they confronted the Maryland team about the graphic to raise concerns. Despite the team being suspended and investigated, Howard’s team said, “True accountability has yet to come.” Howard’s team is asking both UMD and the school’s club tennis executive board to issue public apologies to Howard University and its team, conduct a formal investigation into who created the document, and provide sensitivity training for the school’s team leaders and advisers. The Howard team is also asking that the funds from the weekend tournament be donated to the National Museum of African American History and Culture. “There is no place for racism, intimidation, or imagery rooted in hatred and racial violence in collegiate athletics, on our campuses, or anywhere in our society,” Wayne A. I. Frederick, Howard University interim president and president emeritus, said in a statement. He added that he appreciated UMD President Darryll J. Pines for his immediate concern and said Howard is there to support all students who participated in the tournament. The Black Student Union at UMD said in a statement posted to its Instagram that the vice president of student affairs reached out to the group directly after the incident. The group thanked the university for its quick response but added, “We know administrative actions alone cannot undo the emotional impact inflicted upon Black students, especially when added to a broader societal climate where racial tension is already a constant weight.” It asked the university to “commit to long-term systemic accountability and active harm restoration, ensuring that the impact on Black students is addressed directly, transparently, and with immediate urgency.”

articles.body: A passengers aboard the flydubai flight on which Indian captain Smit Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot have alleged that members of the cabin crew attempted to loosen the accused attacker’s restraints and tried to put a mysterious pill into the injured pilot’s mouth.Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, passenger Rajuan said he suspected some crew members may have assisted the attacker, identified as Omani national Hammam al-Hammami. He described confrontations with attendants, their attempts to prevent passengers from filming and exchanges between the crew members and the accused that left him fearing the danger had not passed even after the co-pilot was restrained.According to Rajuan’s account to the Israeli newspaper, crew members repeatedly confronted passengers who tried to record the incident. One attendant allegedly asked him whether he was a police officer. He also described attempts to grab and pull at clothing, adding to his suspicion that the crew’s actions were unusual.The passenger further alleged that the crew tried to loosen al-Hammami’s restraints and attempted to administer an unidentified pill to Machchhar, who had been injured during the alleged attack. Rajuan also claimed that the flight had been staffed exclusively by male attendants, raising questions about whether the accused could have had assistance from within the crew.The claims come amid reports that two Maldivian pilots employed by flydubai have been arrested by UAE police in connection with the investigation. Maldivian news portal Adhadhu reported that the two were taken into custody on October 3 and that their families were informed through the Maldivian Embassy in the UAE. Authorities have not disclosed the allegations against them or confirmed the nature of their suspected links to the incident.Flight FZ1073 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers and crew members when al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar with an axe in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft. Despite his injuries, the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. The aircraft was subsequently diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing.Reports have also suggested that al-Hammami had planned the alleged attack before joining Flydubai and intended to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport in Israel. articles.title: Trial hears woman recall fan falling on her at Ipswich Town v Maidstone
articles.summary: A man is accused of assault after falling from the upper tier at Ipswich Town on to home supporters.
articles.body:
A woman has told a jury she thought she "could have died" when a football fan fell on to her from the upper tier of a grandstand during a match.

Joanne Peters, who has the back condition scoliosis, was injured when 62-year-old John Ryan landed on her at Ipswich Town's Portman Road ground in January 2024.

Ipswich Crown Court heard how Peters initially thought the box behind her had collapsed and she had been left "terrified" by the impact.

Ryan, of Railway Street, Chatham, Kent, denies one count of assault by beating and one count of actual bodily harm. The jury has retired to consider its verdicts.

Ryan had been one of thousands of Maidstone United supporters who saw their non-league club win 2-1 in the FA Cup .

The court heard he had been celebrating a goal in the Cobbold Stand upper tier above Peters when he fell, slid down a sloping roof and landed on the Ipswich supporters below.

"I thought the box behind us had collapsed into us," Peters tearfully told the court.

"It was terrifying... just a really, really scary situation.

"He landed on my shoulder. The pressure of that fall — he could have broken my neck."

The court heard Peters suffered "elements of whiplash" as well as numbness in her hands and internal bruising.

Her partner Aaron Rose told the jury he had been kicked in the back of the head.

Prosecutor Simon Gladwell previously told the trial Ryan had drunk five cans of lager ahead of the match.

Questioned over whether Ryan was drunk, Rose said he believed he was.

"I've been around drunk people, and my assumption is that he was," he said.

"The way he acted towards stewards after — it wouldn't take a scientist to work it out."

Ryan told the court the game had been "the biggest match in the club's history" and he had been celebrating the "special" goal.

"Everyone's jumping about, and you just go where you go," he said of that goal celebration.

"I don't know if I bumped somebody or my foot slipped or what; I just ended up going down the stairs.

"I couldn't stop myself; my leg hit that wall... I just started tilting over.

"As I put my arm out, I just started rolling over. There's nothing to hold on to."

The court heard Ryan missed work through his own injuries to his arm and leg.

The prosecution said two other men went on to the roof at the same time as Ryan, but were stopped from going further.

The prosecutor questioned why Ryan had moved toward the roof during the celebration and argued he had done so purposefully.

Ryan responded with: "No. It wasn't like that.

"All I know is that I ended up going down the steps and I couldn't stop myself.

Ryan had originally been standing trial on two counts of assault by beating, but one has been dropped.

articles.title: Jury selection to begin in federal hate crimes trial over Buffalo, N.Y., supermarket shooting
articles.summary: For Wayne Jones, discussing the horrific supermarket shooting in Buffalo, N.Y., in which a white supremacist killed 10 people, including his mother Celestine Chaney, has taken over much of his life these past four years.
articles.body: For Wayne Jones, discussing the horrific supermarket shooting in Buffalo, N.Y., in which a white supremacist killed 10 people, including his mother Celestine Chaney, has taken over much of his life these past four years. He can numbly list talking points for media and gun violence panels. But thinking about her absence each day is one reason why Jones would not want to see the shooter sentenced to death. “I really think that he should just sit and have to think about it year after year after year and just be miserable,” said Jones, who plans to attend the trial. “When I was younger, I probably was more prone to say ‘kill him.’ But, at this point, I mean, he’s still got well another 20-30 years of appeals.” Jury selection is set to begin Tuesday in the federal trial in which Payton Gendron faces a potential death penalty. The attack at the Tops Friendly Market in 2022 is believed to be the deadliest hate-motivated shooting targeting Black people by a lone gunman in the last century. Gendron is facing over two dozen federal hate crime charges and more than a dozen firearms charges. He is already spending life in prison after pleading guilty to state murder charges in a 2023 trial where he tearfully admitted to the crimes and renounced his past views. His defense team is not going to dispute his guilt. Their sole objective is to ensure Gendron is spared from execution. “Nothing will change the fact that Payton Gendron will die in prison,” the federal public defender office said in a statement. “At trial, we will offer mitigating evidence about Payton that the jury needs to consider in making its decision. Nothing we say or do is intended to be disrespectful or insensitive to the victims, the survivors, or their loved ones.” Some victims’ family members, however, are not totally against the death penalty. “I’ve never been like out here like, ‘Yay! Go for the death penalty.’ That’s never been me,” said Buffalo Common Council member Zeneta Everhart, who ran for office over a year after her son, Zaire, survived the shooting. “Ten people died that day in an egregious way and in an awful, terrible, traumatic way.” Her son, now 25, and the two other survivors have had their lives irrevocably altered, she added. How racist conspiracy theories played a role in the attack On May 14, 2022, a then-18-year-old Gendron drove over 200 miles (320 kilometers) from his home in Conklin, a predominantly white and rural town, to Buffalo. He fired around 60 shots from a semiautomatic rifle at employees and shoppers. Video revealed Gendron apologized to a white store worker after shooting him in the leg. He surrendered to police as he exited the supermarket. Investigators found past social media posts and other writings by Gendron dedicated to planning an attack to frighten people who were non-white and non-Christian into leaving the U.S. He also promoted a baseless “great replacement theory” that people of color will replace white people through higher birth rates and immigration. The victims who were killed were all Black and between ages 32 and 86. Besides Chaney, they included Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, church deacon Heyward Patterson, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison and Aaron Salter, a retired Buffalo police officer who was working as a security guard. Under President Joe Biden, the U.S. Justice Department in 2024 decided to pursue a death sentence. It was the first capital case overseen by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, who had previously put a moratorium on the death penalty. Gendron and his legal team relayed that he would only plead guilty in his federal case in exchange for a life sentence. The Justice Department rejected that proposal. Anti-Black crimes still lead in hate crime data The 2022 shooting stands apart as one of the deadliest acts of anti-Black violence in modern U.S. history. It also reflects a grim reality represented in national bias crime statistics. Black people have comprised the “no. 1 numerical target” annually since the FBI began collecting data in 1991, hate crime analyst Brian Levin, of the California Association of Human Relations Organizations, said. The record high was 3,670 anti-Black bias incidents in 1996. According to FBI data released in August, law enforcement agencies reported over 2,800 anti-Black hate crime incidents in 2025, nearly three times the number targeting Latinos. The FBI also reported a 7% decline in hate crime incidents from 2024 to 2025. The Buffalo shooting and the 2015 Charleston, S.C., church shooting, in which a white gunman killed nine Black churchgoers, show how online radicalization makes this a terrorism matter as well. “Unfortunately, he (Gendron) fits the pattern of young, mostly white males undertaking targeted massacres which are then justified by manifestos, which are also part of a continuing chain that references prior attacks often but seeks to encourage future ones,” Levin said. Everhart, whose son still has shrapnel in his body after being shot in the neck, says hate crime enhancements might be the only deterrent. “This isn’t a shooting over a robbery or a domestic violence situation. This is domestic terrorism,” Everhart said. “It is important we go after the death penalty in this case. But if he doesn’t end up getting it, I know that justice will be served.” Garnell Whitfield lost his 86-year-old mother Ruth in the shooting. He has no thoughts on whether capital punishment should be issued because “this is the federal government doing what they deem they have to do.” He’s spent the past four years honoring his mother’s memory by working with church groups, victims’ rights groups, gun lobbyists and others to address white nationalist movements and racial violence. Whitfield said he hopes trial testimony reveals more about “the support that he (Gendron) might have had, the radicalization, social media and societal ills that caused people to hate and be violent that are inherent in our society” that preceded the killing. “Those are the things that I care about,” he said.

articles.title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
articles.summary: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.
articles.body: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings. A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology. Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission. “There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.” Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating. That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey. Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her. The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam. “I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.” Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview. Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000. “I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.” Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature. This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively. Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance. “Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.” The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish. It found that during the third quarter of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users. Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts. The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns. Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors. One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts. Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.” “That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.” Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began. Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.” “They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

articles.title: Houthis threaten Saudi Arabia’s Aramco facilities and airports
articles.summary: Explosions in Sanaa reported shortly after Saudi-led coalition’s evacuation order as Houthis promise ‘harsh’ response.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis have warned all employees and civilians near Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities to evacuate, calling the sites “a legitimate target”.

The warning on Tuesday from the group’s spokesman, Yahya Saree, was prompted by an evacuation order from the Saudi-led coalition urging civilians to evacuate Yemeni Oil Company’s al-Sabah central station in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa.

Shortly after the Saudi-led coalition’s evacuation order, Al Jazeera’s team on the ground reported hearing explosions in Sanaa. Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis said air strikes by the Saudi-backed forces struck an oil facility in the al-Sabaha area of the capital.

“We heard the explosion upon Saudi Arabia targeting the Yemeni oil al-Sabah Central Station here in the capital Sanaa,” Al Jazeera correspondent Yousef Mawry said.

Saudi Arabia also conducted two other air strike campaigns on the Ras Isa port targeting Yemeni oil storage tanks and on an oil station in the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah province, according to Mawry.

Following the reported explosions, Saree said Houthi fighters were confronting Saudi-backed forces in Sanaa.

Saree responded to the coalition’s evacuation order, warning that any strikes on Sanaa would be met with a “harsh and painful” response in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh.

In a statement on X, Saree said the Houthis would target the sites that were ordered to be evacuated if the Saudi-led coalition proceeded with an attack on Sanaa.

Civilians were told to evacuate the Aramco Company headquarters in Dammam, King Khalid International Airport and a refinery affiliated with Aramco in Riyadh.

“The Ansar Allah Houthi group have not yet launched any attacks, but people are expecting there to be retaliations,” Mawry said.

An attack on King Khalid airport on Saturday left at least 13 people dead and more than 300 injured, rocking the world’s top crude oil exporter. Another person was killed, and 11 were wounded on Sunday after a projectile struck the airport in Riyadh.

Many international airlines have since suspended flights to Saudi ⁠⁠Arabia and ⁠⁠neighbouring countries following the deadly weekend attacks by the Houthis, including Air France-KLM, Air India, Etihad, Lufthansa, Delta, Gulf Air and Qatar Airways.

The kingdom, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, was still weathering new attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.

Saree also reiterated the Houthis’ warning to airports in Saudi Arabia following recent attacks on multiple airports and oil facilities across the country since last week in a spillover from the wider regional conflict between the US and Iran.

Saudi Arabia has in recent ⁠⁠weeks launched strikes against the Houthis and is backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive known as the “Dawn of Yemen” after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast ‌‌last month.

Saudi Arabia’s cabinet, chaired ⁠by Crown Prince ⁠Mohammed bin Salman, said on Tuesday the Houthis would face “consequences” for their attacks across the kingdom, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

articles.title: Why billions spent on defense haven’t shielded Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars on defense every year, but is struggling to protect key assets such as airports, refineries and pipelines from missiles and drones fired by Houthi militants from Yemen.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars on defense every year, but is struggling to protect key assets such as airports, refineries and pipelines from missiles and drones fired by Houthi militants from Yemen. Despite acquiring state-of-the-art weapons systems from the United States and Europe and possessing multi-layered air defenses, the kingdom has seen deadly attacks on the main airport serving the capital, Riyadh, over the past week. Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom. But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides. From the east, Iran fired about 1,000 missiles and drones at Saudi targets during the most intense part of the conflict this year. From the north, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq have sent drones to attack the country’s critical East-West oil pipeline. And from the south, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels fire missiles at the kingdom from shelters and mobile launchers in the mountains of Yemen. Defending Saudi Arabia means protecting a vast network of targets, not just Riyadh or a single refinery. Its defenses must detect incoming threats, decide which to intercept and warn civilians, all within moments, according to Vision2030.ai, an independent website analyzing the kingdom’s economic transformation. The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through. The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack, according to a Saudi source. Houthi capabilities The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses. The approach resembles Russia’s playbook: Moscow has frequently used a mass of drones along with cruise and ballistic missiles in barrages against Ukraine. Cruise missiles fly at lower altitudes, making them harder to identify and track. The Houthis have also introduced a new generation of ballistic missiles that they claim are maneuverable. No single air defense system can guarantee that every incoming threat will be intercepted. But the Houthis have not done this alone. Eight years ago, UN experts “identified missile remnants, related military equipment and military unmanned aerial vehicles that are of Iranian origin and were introduced into Yemen” despite an international arms embargo. That same panel said two years ago that “the scale, nature and extent of transfers of diverse military material and technology provided to the Houthis from external sources, including financial support and training of its combatants, is unprecedented.” Experts note that the latest Houthi missiles, such as the Hatem-2 and the Palestine-2, are very similar in design to Iranian weapons. They are fast and accurate. Last year, a Houthi missile evaded Israel’s vaunted air defenses and impacted near Ben Gurion airport. Analyst Amir Bar Shalom told CNN at the time: “They were very accurate, and to be very accurate if you’re launching from 2,000 kilometers, it’s impressive.” The Houthis have also modified Iranian air defense weapons to strike aircraft and cruise missiles, according to Brigadier General Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces. “These missiles move around for a period of up to 25 minutes per missile and operate using a thermal-tracking system,” he said last month. Will they listen to Tehran? The Houthis have long been part of Iran’s ‘axis of resistance.’ While other allied groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and militias in Iraq have been significantly degraded, the Houthis have gone from strength to strength. They continue to have a strong relationship with Tehran and sent a delegation to the funeral of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. But they also have their own agenda. Seven years of conflict with Saudi Arabia between 2015 and 2022 caused immense suffering in Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, and an economic and transport embargo has continued since. Ultimately, that led the Houthis in July to declare they would attack Saudi shipping in the Red Sea – and the campaign of missile strikes began soon afterwards, initially targeting an Aramco oil refinery on the Red Sea coast and Saudi airbases. The Houthis are demanding an end to Saudi airstrikes in support of government forces in Yemen, as well as billions of dollars in compensation from Saudi Arabia. Whether in good faith or not, Iran has offered to mediate between Riyadh and the Houthis. On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was ready to provide “any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen,” meaning the Houthis. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, claimed Monday that Riyadh had accepted mediation but the group had rejected truce proposals of two weeks and of one month. “The battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena,” al-Bukhaiti said. “Every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow.” Kingdom faces tough choices Saudi Arabia has tried to project an image of “business as usual” even as the conflict with the Houthis intensified. Its civil defense authority stopped issuing public alerts by phone of incoming missiles and drones last week – before the series of deadly strikes on Riyadh airport. Alerts have since resumed, according to several residents of Riyadh who spoke with CNN. Saudi authorities say three ballistic missiles were intercepted on Monday. An expatriate resident of Riyadh told CNN their children were being schooled at home this week. The resident was upset on Saturday by the lack of automatic alerts for incoming missiles in the preceding days but said phone alerts were working effectively by Monday. They also expressed frustration at the Saudi authorities’ silence over the weekend about the strikes on Riyadh airport. CNN has asked the Saudi authorities for a response on the absence of alerts. Going forward, the kingdom faces tough choices. Accommodation with the Houthis after more than a dozen civilians were killed in the airport attacks would be unpalatable. Escalation, through even more intense airstrikes, would bring the risk of further missile attacks that would undermine the goal of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to make Saudi Arabia a world-class destination for investment, technology and tourism. The stakes extend beyond the oil industry. Data centers, desalination plants and airports underpin the kingdom’s technology ambitions, water supply and tourism economy. The crown prince’s marquee investment event in Riyadh later this month will put his pitch to international investors in the spotlight. But major corporations shied away this week from the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh. Defeating the Houthi rebels through a ground offensive involving Yemeni government forces seems highly unlikely. The Houthis are entrenched, battle-hardened and know the mountainous terrain. They have inflicted heavy losses on government forces in the last month. Last year, the US spent more than $1 billion on a seven-week campaign of air-strikes against the Houthis. The Houthis eventually agreed not to attack US shipping in the Red Sea but remained very much in place – and in the meantime shot down a number of highly advanced US Reaper drones. Neither US nor Israeli strikes eliminated members of the Houthi leadership, even if commanders and technocrats were killed. If anything, the Houthis, who may have as many as 350,000 men under arms, are on the front foot. They have now encircled the government-held city of Taiz, Yemen’s third largest and a vital logistical hub, the Institute for the Study of War said on Monday. Saudi Arabia seeks support The Saudis are seeking to mobilize an international coalition against the Houthis. Regional allies have offered help in the way of defensive systems. Pakistan has sent thousands of troops to help defend the kingdom. Egypt has offered whatever support is asked for. The Saudis may also be able to procure more air defense systems from Europe and the US, after running down shipments delivered at the start of the conflict with Iran. But the US itself is short of such systems. A report by the US Defense Department’s Inspector-General said the campaign against Iran had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.” And with mid-term elections three weeks away, US President Donald Trump is wary of yet another entanglement in the Middle East. He has been non-committal about direct US strikes against the Houthis, while not ruling them out. “US reluctance to get involved stokes the perception that the United States has abandoned a partner at its moment of greatest need,” according to Michael Ratney at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. Writing before the airport strikes, Ratney – a former US ambassador in Riyadh – added: “The kingdom is under attack, and as a political matter, it has to retaliate. But ultimately, we should expect a return to diplomacy – imperfect, unsatisfying diplomacy that nonetheless deescalates the conflict.” That may leave the Houthis in place, and in a stronger position inside Yemen. CNN’s Nic Robertson contributed to this article.

articles.title: Sean McVay is 'sick' about his overtime call as another Super Bowl coach publicly regrets end of game decision
articles.summary: Sean McVay says he's "sick" after a third-down play call led to a blocked field goal in the Rams' overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills on Monday.
articles.body: Week 5 of this NFL season will be remembered by historians as the week when head coaches apologized, admitted mistakes and otherwise regretted their decisions in front of their teams and in public — and Los Angeles Rams coach Sean McVay is the latest to join them. The Rams lost in overtime to the Buffalo Bills in what was perhaps the most entertaining game of the season on Monday Night Football. Afterward, McVay was unhappy with himself, saying he was "sick" and "regretting" a decision that wasn’t necessarily wrong but wasn’t optimal and didn’t help his team in what could have been a game-deciding situation. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Here's the situation: The game is in overtime. The Rams have stopped the Bills on their first possession, so any points by McVay's team wins the game. And the Rams seem headed toward those points and victory when they drive from their 20-yard line to the Buffalo 30 mostly by attempting five consecutive pass plays. The Buffalo defense is on its heels under Matthew Stafford’s passing barrage. But on third-and-5 from the Bills' 30-yard line, McVay calls a run for Kyren Williams off right tackle. No gain. It was, clearly, the coach setting his team up for a field goal rather than pressing the issue. Except the Rams had their field goal blocked on fourth down, continuing a multi-season struggle with their special teams that has cost them multiple games. "Yeah, you know what? If I would have known," McVay told reporters afterward. "I wish I would have had a better play call and gone for it, got it a lot tighter. I'm sick right now with myself. "...I'm proud of the way that we battled and I'm sick that we came up short and I'll be regretting kicking that and not having a better call to be able to go forward on third down ... "That's on me." We heard this multiple times in Week 5. Washington Commanders coach Dan Quinn said "it's my responsibility" for the blown clock management at the end of his team's game against the New York Giants that turned a likely victory into a tie. Philadelphia Eagles coach Nick Sirianni took blame for his team's last-second loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars because of a decision he made on a kickoff. "I lost us that game," Sirianni said. NICK SIRIANNI MAKES DECISON THAT OPENED THE DOOR TO A JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS COMEBACK WIN These coaches are seemingly wrestling each other for Harry Truman's "The Buck Stops Here" Oval Office sign. And that's good. Accountability from a head coach, especially when it is taken publicly, sets a good example for players and how they'll act privately within the team. But that's not the point. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The point is three coaches that took teams to the Super Bowl — McVay and Sirianni won on the NFL's grandest stage — made significant errors on the same week of NFL action. The mistakes were so obvious that all decided to take responsibility publicly. The NFL last week was mired in officials making mistakes and getting suspended and that was the big story. These star coaches all blowing it on the same week has shifted the focus to the quality of decisions by coaches in the league. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO
